unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.prompt: A corridor smoke detector is in alarm and you can see gray smoke at the far end of the floor. You are the unarmed officer on post. What should you do first?

options.a: Start the fire-evacuation plan, close doors if safe, and meet the fire department
options.b: Silence the fire panel first so you can search the floor alone for the burning source
options.c: Load occupants into passenger elevators so they can leave the high-rise faster
options.d: Hold people at their desks until a second detector or a 911 callback confirms fire

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: Visible smoke plus an active fire alarm is treated as a real fire. Unarmed officers start the posted evacuation, close doors behind them if it is safe (to slow smoke spread), and meet the fire department with access and location information. Searching alone after silencing the panel, using elevators, or waiting for a second confirmation burns escape time.

distractorExplanations.b: Silencing a panel with smoke showing delays evacuation and can hide later alarms from the fire service.
distractorExplanations.c: Elevators can stall or open onto a fire floor; occupants use stairs unless firefighters direct otherwise.
distractorExplanations.d: Smoke already confirms the emergency; waiting for a second alarm wastes the time people need to get out.

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.prompt: A visitor in your lobby is pale, sweating, and clutching the center of the chest. They ask you to “just give it a minute.” What is the correct unarmed-officer response?

options.a: Drive them to the emergency room in a personal car so they skip the ambulance wait
options.b: Call 911, stay with them, send trained staff for the AED, and keep the crowd back
options.c: Walk them to the restroom and wait ten minutes to see whether the chest pain eases
options.d: Have them lie down, offer leftover desk aspirin, and call 911 only if symptoms worsen

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: Chest pain with sweating is treated as a possible heart attack. The officer’s job is to get EMS en route immediately, stay with the person, fetch an AED if trained staff can use it, and keep bystanders from crowding the scene. Driving the patient, waiting it out, or improvising medication delays professional care and adds liability.

distractorExplanations.a: A private-car transport delays EMS treatment and monitoring; call 911 and wait with the person on site.
distractorExplanations.c: Delaying for the pain to pass is a common mistake; minutes of untreated cardiac symptoms worsen outcomes.
distractorExplanations.d: Unprescribed aspirin and a wait-and-see plan are not a substitute for activating 911 at the first sign of a heart attack.

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.prompt: You hear what sound like gunshots in the parking garage. You are unarmed at the lobby desk with a radio. What is your role?

options.a: Sweep each garage level with a flashlight until you locate and stop the attacker yourself
options.b: Herd everyone into the open glass lobby so you can take a complete tenant headcount
options.c: Direct people to run or lock down as trained, then report what you see from cover
options.d: Move to the garage ramp and confront the attacker with your baton, radio, and flashlight

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: An unarmed officer is not a SWAT element. The trained response is to get people out of the kill zone or into a locked room, then give police a clear location and description from cover. Hunting the attacker, massing people in an open lobby, or confronting with a flashlight or baton turns the officer into another victim and can draw fire onto bystanders.

distractorExplanations.a: Room-to-room search is a police/tactical task; unarmed guards observe, report, and help people avoid the threat.
distractorExplanations.b: Clustering people in an open lobby creates one large target; follow run/hide/lockdown, not a public headcount.
distractorExplanations.d: Confronting an armed attacker with a baton is last-resort self-defense only, not the planned unarmed response.

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.prompt: The lobby phone rings. The caller says a bomb will go off in the building this afternoon and then pauses. How should you handle the call?

options.a: Hang up quickly so the lobby line stays free when police try to call the site back
options.b: Pull the fire alarm immediately so every floor empties by the nearest stairwell
options.c: Transfer the caller to the property manager and drop off as soon as they pick up
options.d: Keep the caller on the line, fill the threat checklist, then notify police and a supervisor

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: A bomb-threat call is an intelligence opportunity. Stay on the line, stall for details (location, time, voice, background noise), and fill the site checklist while a second person notifies police and a supervisor. Evacuation routing is a command decision because the fire-alarm path may walk people past a device. Transferring or hanging up loses the caller.

distractorExplanations.a: Ending the call to “free the line” throws away voice, timing, and location clues the checklist is built to capture.
distractorExplanations.b: A fire-alarm dump can route occupants past the device; police/command decide whether and how to evacuate.
distractorExplanations.c: Transferring risks losing the caller entirely; the person who took the call completes the checklist.

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.prompt: A small trash-can fire is burning in an occupied office. You are trained on the extinguisher, the fire is still in the can, and the exit path behind you is clear. What is appropriate?

options.a: Use PASS on the extinguisher if the fire stays small, then report it and watch for rekindle
options.b: Carry the burning can down the occupied corridor and dump it in the parking lot
options.c: Prop the office door wide open so smoke can vent while you go look for a supervisor
options.d: Throw a mop-bucket of water on it because office paper will go out with enough water

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: Incipient, contained fires may be fought with a proper extinguisher when the officer is trained, has a clear escape path, and the fire is not spreading. PASS (pull, aim, squeeze, sweep) is the method, and the event still gets reported because of rekindle and fire-code follow-up. Moving a burning can, ventilating into a corridor, or using random water are not fire-extinguisher practice.

distractorExplanations.b: Carrying a burning container spreads fire and smoke through the means of egress.
distractorExplanations.c: Propping the door feeds oxygen and pushes smoke into the corridor; close the door after a safe attempt.
distractorExplanations.d: Water is wrong for some fuels and is not a substitute for a rated extinguisher used with PASS.

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.prompt: An employee collapses in the break room, is unresponsive, and is not breathing normally. What should the unarmed officer do?

options.a: Splash cold water on their face and wait several minutes to see if they sit up on their own
options.b: Call 911, start CPR if trained, send someone for the AED, and keep the scene clear
options.c: Drag them to the loading-dock door so the ambulance crew can see them from the street
options.d: Sit them upright against the wall to “open the airway” and skip chest compressions

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: Unresponsive and not breathing normally is a cardiac-arrest presentation. Activate EMS, begin CPR if you are trained, and get an AED on the chest as soon as it arrives. Do not wait for them to “come around,” move them unless the scene is unsafe, or sit them up—those delays cost the minutes CPR and defibrillation are meant to buy.

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting for a spontaneous recovery wastes the time when CPR and an AED can restart circulation.
distractorExplanations.c: Dragging an unresponsive person can worsen injury and delays CPR; EMS comes to the patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Sitting an unresponsive, non-breathing person upright does not replace compressions or an AED.

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.prompt: A tenant reports an unlabeled backpack left against a column near the main entrance, with no owner in sight after a radio query. What should you do?

options.a: Pick it up and shake it so you can tell whether anything inside feels like a bomb
options.b: Carry the backpack to the dumpster so any hazard sits outside the occupied floors
options.c: Keep people back, leave it untouched, radio a description, and wait for bomb technicians
options.d: Open the zipper a few inches and photograph the contents for tonight’s written incident report

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: Unattended suspicious items are isolate-and-report problems, not handle-and-inspect problems. Unarmed officers deny the area, leave the item in place, describe it and its location to police, and let bomb technicians decide. Handling, moving, or opening the bag can complete a circuit or put the officer in the blast radius.

distractorExplanations.a: Shaking a bag can detonate an improvised device; do not touch or test the item.
distractorExplanations.b: Moving a suspected device through occupied space is how a lobby problem becomes a whole-building problem.
distractorExplanations.d: Opening it for photos is still handling; documentation is done from a distance after specialists clear it.

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.prompt: Police radio traffic says an active shooter may be on floor 4 of your building. You are unarmed at the ground-floor desk. What should you do from that post?

options.a: Take the stairs to floor 4 to find the subject and stall them until police can arrive
options.b: Announce over the PA the name of a tenant you think might be the active shooter
options.c: Unlock all stair doors so anyone can move freely between floors during the shooting
options.d: Stop inbound visitors, lock the lobby per plan, and give police location updates from cover

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: From a lobby post the unarmed officer’s value is access control and information: keep new people from walking into the event, follow the lockdown plan, and give police what you can see or hear without becoming a target. Going to floor 4 to “stall” the shooter, naming a suspect on the PA, or unlocking vertical circulation works against police control of the scene.

distractorExplanations.a: Moving toward the shooter to delay them is a police/tactical role, not an unarmed observe-and-report job.
distractorExplanations.b: Broadcasting a guessed identity can panic occupants and contaminate the police response.
distractorExplanations.c: Unlocking stairs can give the attacker more mobility; follow the site lockdown, do not improvise free movement.

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.prompt: Outdoor warning sirens sound and the weather radio says a tornado warning includes your site. Occupants are asking where to go. What do you direct?

options.a: Move people to the marked lowest interior shelter, away from windows and lobby glass
options.b: Send everyone to their cars in the lot so they can drive out of the warned area
options.c: Move the crowd to the roof deck so they can watch which way the storm is tracking
options.d: Open every exterior door so indoor and outdoor air pressure can equalize in the storm

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: Tornado shelter is the lowest interior space the site has marked—typically an interior corridor, restroom core, or basement—away from glass. Vehicles, roofs, and open lots expose people to debris. Opening exterior doors is an old myth and can let wind and glass into the shelter path. The officer’s job is to move people to the posted shelter and keep them there until the warning expires or emergency management says otherwise.

distractorExplanations.b: Cars offer little protection from tornado debris; driving during a warning puts people in the hazard.
distractorExplanations.c: Upper floors and roofs take the worst wind; shelter is down and interior, not up and outside.
distractorExplanations.d: Opening doors to “equalize pressure” is a myth that lets debris and wind into occupied space.

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.prompt: Two riders are stuck between floors in a passenger elevator and are calling on the car phone, frightened but uninjured. What should you do?

options.a: Pry the lobby landing doors with a tool to create an opening they can climb through
options.b: Call elevator service and fire, keep talking to the riders, and do not force the doors
options.c: Climb in through the top hatch from the floor above so you can pull the riders out
options.d: Tell them most cars restart within an hour and to call back only if they are still stuck

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: Elevator rescue is for licensed mechanics and the fire department. The officer’s job is to notify the right responders immediately, stay on the phone to keep riders calm and informed, and keep untrained staff from prying doors or entering the hoistway. Delay is dangerous if a rider has a medical issue; forcing doors risks a fall into the shaft.

distractorExplanations.a: Forcing landing doors can drop someone into the hoistway; that opening is for trained rescuers only.
distractorExplanations.c: Entering through the hatch is a fall and crush hazard; unarmed officers do not perform hoistway rescues.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting an hour ignores medical risk in the car; call service or fire as soon as you know they are trapped.

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.prompt: You smell a sharp chemical odor at a lab loading dock and see a wet patch on the concrete with no posted product name. Staff are still working in the bay. What should you do?

options.a: Mop the unknown puddle with water and a shop rag so the smell fades before the next truck
options.b: Prop both dock doors so the fumes blow down the interior corridor and out through the lobby
options.c: Stop work, isolate the bay, evacuate per the HAZMAT plan, and call specialists—do not clean it
options.d: Keep the dock crew on task and wait fifteen minutes to see whether anyone develops symptoms

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: Unknown chemical odor plus a spill is a HAZMAT scene. Unarmed officers isolate, deny entry, follow the site evacuation for that dock, and call the people who read SDS and wear the right PPE. Cleanup, water, or corridor ventilation can spread the product or react with it. Waiting for symptoms makes the first patients your own staff.

distractorExplanations.a: Unknown chemicals can be toxic or water-reactive; mopping is for trained HAZMAT, not a security mop job.
distractorExplanations.b: Propping doors can push fumes into occupied interior space instead of containing them at the dock.
distractorExplanations.d: Using workers as a detection system delays evacuation; isolate and call specialists at the first unknown spill.

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.prompt: At a concert vehicle gate the crowd behind the magnetometers starts to surge forward. People at the front cannot step back. What should you do?

options.a: Close and lock the vehicle gate to stop the crowd’s forward push until the surge calms
options.b: Push the front row backward with your hands to create a gap at the magnetometer line
options.c: Cut the overhead lights so people will freeze and stop moving toward the checkpoint
options.d: Open extra lanes if you can, give loud directions, and radio for more staff

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: Crowd crush is a pressure problem. Relieve it by widening flow, communicating, and getting more staff—not by adding a closed barrier, shoving the front, or killing the lights. Closing a gate during a surge stacks people against metal. Darkness causes trips. The unarmed officer’s job is to reduce density and call for help before injuries start.

distractorExplanations.a: Locking the gate during a surge builds pressure against it and is a classic crush setup.
distractorExplanations.b: Shoving the front row compresses the people behind them; relieve pressure by opening flow, not by pushing.
distractorExplanations.c: Darkness causes panic and falls; keep lighting and give directions people can see and hear.

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.prompt: A parent at your mall post says their seven-year-old walked out of a store two minutes ago and is not answering a phone. What should you do?

options.a: Wait thirty minutes at the security desk in case the child is still in a fitting room
options.b: Call the missing-child code now with a description, cover exits, and pull cameras
options.c: Walk every store on the concourse yourself before putting any code on the radio
options.d: Page the child’s full name over the PA and wait at lost-and-found for a parent reply

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: A missing-child report is an immediate code, not a wait-and-see. Broadcast a description, put people on exits, and use cameras while others search. Minutes of delay let a child—or someone with the child—leave the building. A solo store walk or a name-only page without exit coverage is too slow and too leaky.

distractorExplanations.a: A 30-minute wait is how a child leaves the property; missing-child codes start at once.
distractorExplanations.c: A store-by-store search before the code leaves exits uncovered; call the code first, then search.
distractorExplanations.d: Paging a name without covering doors is passive and can also publicize a child’s identity to the wrong people.

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.prompt: After a fall in the lobby there is a pool of blood on the tile. The injured person has left with EMS. How should you handle the spill?

options.a: Dry-mop the blood into a regular trash bag so the lobby looks clean for the next visitors
options.b: Wipe it with paper towels in bare hands, then use desk sanitizer as if that were enough PPE
options.c: Block the area, put on PPE, and clean it with the bloodborne kit and labeled bags
options.d: Leave the pool overnight and let the morning janitorial crew treat it as ordinary dirt

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: Blood on a public floor is an OSHA bloodborne-pathogens cleanup, not ordinary housekeeping. Isolate the area, wear the kit PPE, use the disinfectant and biohazard bags the site stocks, and log the exposure-control steps. Bare hands, regular trash, or leaving it until morning all create an exposure for staff and the public.

distractorExplanations.a: Blood is regulated waste; a dry mop and ordinary trash do not meet the bloodborne-pathogen standard.
distractorExplanations.b: Bare-hand contact is an exposure; gloves and the rest of the BBP kit are required.
distractorExplanations.d: A lobby blood spill is an immediate exposure risk, not a next-shift housekeeping ticket.

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.prompt: A high-rise loses utility power at 21:00. Emergency lights flicker on. Tenants are asking whether to use the elevators. What should you do?

options.a: Reset the fire pumps and the fire-alarm panel as if those life-safety panels were ordinary breakers
options.b: Send every remaining tenant home and padlock the building until the utility restores power at dawn
options.c: Ride each passenger elevator to every floor so you can inspect the shaft and cars in person
options.d: Check emergency lighting, listen for trapped cars, and follow the generator/engineer plan

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: A high-rise blackout is a life-safety check, not a DIY electrical reset. Confirm emergency lighting, treat elevators as possible entrapments (call boxes and positions, do not joyride them), and follow the posted generator and engineer notification. Fire pumps and alarm panels are not power resets. Evacuation or lock-up is a plan decision after those checks, not the first move.

distractorExplanations.a: Tampering with fire pumps or the alarm panel can disable life-safety systems that must stay up in a blackout.
distractorExplanations.b: Mass lock-up or send-home is not automatic; first verify lighting, elevators, and the generator SOP.
distractorExplanations.c: Riding elevators during a power failure risks adding another stalled car; check for entrapments from the lobby.
